title: Demonstrate an understanding of fruit cultivars

lessons.title: What a cultivar is
lessons.html:
Kinds and cultivars

An apple is a kind of fruit. But there are many different apples. Some are red, some are green. Some are sweet, some are sour. Some are picked early in summer and others late in autumn. Each of these different types is called a cultivar (cultivated variety).

Well-known apple cultivars grown in South Africa include Granny Smith (green), Golden Delicious (yellow), Royal Gala and Fuji (red-striped) and Pink Lady. Common pear cultivars include Packham's Triumph, Forelle and Williams Bon Chretien. Plums, peaches, nectarines, apricots, cherries and table grapes also have many cultivars.

How cultivars differ

  • Colour of the skin and flesh.
  • Shape and size of the fruit.
  • Taste: sweet, sour, juicy, crisp.
  • Harvest time: early, mid or late season.
  • Storage: how long the fruit keeps in cold storage.
  • Chilling needs: how much winter cold the tree needs to flower well.
  • Disease and sunburn sensitivity.

Why cultivars matter to you

On the farm each block is planted with a certain cultivar. Each cultivar is picked at its own time and may be handled differently. Mixing cultivars in one bin causes problems at the packhouse, because buyers order fruit by cultivar. Always check the block number and cultivar before you start work and keep cultivars separate.

Learning to recognise cultivars

Look at the fruit shape, colour, stalk, spots on the skin (lenticels) and the shape of the leaves. Ask an experienced worker to show you the differences in each block. With practice you will know them quickly.

lessons.title: Choosing cultivars and pollination
lessons.html:
How farmers choose cultivars

Before planting a new orchard, the farmer chooses cultivars carefully because the trees will be there for many years. Things the farmer looks at:

  • Climate: deciduous fruit trees need cold winters. Areas such as the Ceres, Elgin and Langkloof valleys get more winter cold than warmer areas. A cultivar with high chilling needs will flower poorly in a warm area.
  • Market: what buyers want, locally and overseas.
  • Harvest spread: planting early, mid and late cultivars spreads the picking work and packhouse work over a longer time.
  • Soil and water on the farm, and the rootstock that suits it.
  • Cost and royalties: some new cultivars are protected and the farmer pays a fee to grow them.

Pollination

Many cultivars cannot set fruit with their own pollen. They need pollen from a different, compatible cultivar that flowers at the same time. This is called a pollinator cultivar. For example, many apple and pear blocks have pollinator trees planted in the rows. Bees carry the pollen from flower to flower, so many farms bring in beehives during flowering.

Looking after bees

During flowering, follow the farm rules about spraying, because some sprays can kill bees. Do not disturb hives. If you are allergic to bee stings, tell your supervisor.

Keeping records

The farm keeps a block list with each block's cultivar, rootstock, planting year and pollinators. Labels on rows and maps of the orchard help everyone work in the right place.

SeasonExample task linked to cultivar
SpringCheck flowering of main and pollinator cultivars
Summer to autumnPick each cultivar at its own maturity
WinterPrune each cultivar according to how it bears

Key points

  • A cultivar is a cultivated variety of a fruit kind.
  • Cultivars differ in colour, taste, harvest time, storage and chilling needs.
  • Keep cultivars separate in bins and records.
  • Many cultivars need a pollinator cultivar and bees to set fruit.
  • Farmers choose cultivars for climate, market and harvest spread.
